newsitem.title: ERITREA: Sudan rebel alliance scores with first offensive.
newsitem.headline: Sudan rebel alliance scores with first offensive.

text.p: The Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) dominates a Sudanese rebel alliance that has scored a string of battlefield successes in eastern Sudan in its first major combined offensive.
Sudan's government, however, says National Democratic Alliance (NDA) victories rely on Eritrean and Ethiopian troops fighting alongside the rebels, a charge denied by both Asmara and Addis Ababa.

NDA forces attacked along Sudan's border with Ethiopia on January 12 and seized the border towns of Kurmuk and Qeissan and a string of garrisons in Blue Nile province and further north around the town of Kassala, close to the border with Eritrea.

Bringing together Sudan's northern and southern opposition, the NDA was formed in 1989 but it was only in Asmara in June 1995 that the largest gathering of groups in three years agreed to join their forces and Eritrea gave them bases for training.
They were united by their common desire to put an end to the rule of the National Islamic Front (NIF) and Sudan's military leader Omar Hassan al-Bashir, who seized power in a 1989 coup.
But the NDA was boosted by a headquarters bordering on north Sudan when Eritrea cut diplomatic relations with Khartoum in December 1994 and handed the Sudanese embassy in Asmara to the opposition.
Veteran SPLA commander John Garang was appointed in October last year as chairman of a four-man joint military command to plan and coordinate rebel operations against Khartoum's forces.
The joint military force consists of the SPLA, the Sudan Alliance Forces (SAF) and Beja Congress, from the rugged east.
Garang says the NDA's strategy is to overthrow the Islamist government in Khartoum through military operations in the east and south which will trigger a popular uprising in the capital.
Estimates of the alliance's strength are rare but the SPLA has tens of thousands of fighters based in its traditional stronghold in southern Sudan where it has fought since 1983.

Exiled leaders of Sudan's main northern-based parties, the Umma and the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), and Garang, smaller parties, former senior Sudanese army officers, lawyers and other civic leaders agreed on an NDA manifesto in 1995.
The manifesto says self-determination may be exercised at any time by any people and is a solution to the civil war.

It said following the defeat of Khartoum the people of the mainly Christian and animist south shall exercise the right of self-determination through a referendum before the end of an interim period of rule.
The manifesto ruled out the imposition of Islamic sharia law by Khartoum on the south, saying full equality for citizens had to be guaranteed without discrimination on religious grounds.
The alliance received a big political boost in December when it was joined by former Sudanese prime minister Sadiq Al-Mahdi who fled Khartoum, pledging to fight against it with minimum bloodshed.

Mahdi, great grandson of the Sudanese Mahdi, who rebelled against Egyptian imperialism in the 1880s, is a towering figure in Sudanese politics as head of the Umma, and spiritual leader of the Ansar or Mahdist movement.
Rebellion in the south against rule from the Moslem and Arabised north began in 1957 when Anya Nya rebels fought until an agreement on regional autonomy in 1972 in a war that cost a million lives.
The rank and file of the SPLA are dominated by Garang's own Dinka tribe, seen by most other tribes in the south as a primitive people whose numerical superiority gave them power.

The SPLA splintered into at least four factions and lost territory to Khartoum after its fighters were thrown out of bases in Ethiopia in 1991 with the overthrow of then dictator Mengistu Haile Mariam.
Human rights groups have reported widescale abuses by rebel and government forces including the use of children as fighters.
